items_missed: No 'How are you today?' and no real agenda statement — 'Alright, so I'm ready for the inventory list' is a handoff, not a roadmap, and there was no ~10-15 minute timeframe and no 'sound good?' confirmation.
Never checked availability for the requested Friday, December 11 move date.

Zero pricing delivered on the call. No hourly rate, no day-of-week tier (Dec 11 is a Friday, which is a different rate), no what's-included list — on a call where the customer said 'I just wanna make sure I have all the money set aside for that.'
Customer volunteered that the king bed 'is all wood which will need to be taken apart obviously' and she never confirmed disassembly and reassembly are included at no charge.

No No Worries Damage Coverage — on a move with a 75-80 inch TV, a 50 inch TV, a king bedroom set and a dresser with mirror. Highest-value differentiator on this specific inventory and it was never said.
No Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no no-hidden-fees pitch, no 'pricing is super simple' opener.

Clock mechanics only half-explained — the 2.5-hour minimum was stated, but not that the clock starts on-site when the contract opens, not the 15-minute prorated increments, and no 'does that make sense?' sense-check.
Promised a range and never gave one: 'I'll give you a range, like just in case scenario' — then no time range, no number of movers, ever appeared. The customer asked for hours twice.
No Save Your Ass speech at all, which is the biggest content miss on this call given the customer handed her the setup (see coaching note).
Destination access never probed — the drop-off is a tentative address on an eight-house street, and there was no question about parking, walk distance, stairs at destination, or driveway access.
No booking attempt. The customer said 'we're going to use you all regardless' and she never asked to lock in December 11.
No no-deposit mention, no 'reply with any corrections,' no BOLDED-details framing for the email, no 'any other questions before I let you go?', no business hours.
No insurance conversation of any kind — neither No Worries nor the 60 cents/lb baseline.
top_strength: The inventory intake was genuinely excellent and is the model for how to run this part of a call. She worked the house room by room, then closed with a full verbal read-back — 'we've got the laundry, the three bedrooms in the kitchen... the garage we have the two deep freezers in the garage shelf' — which is exactly what caught the fridge and the tools the customer had forgotten. She also probed the gaps he had not thought of ('what about like bins, any extra stock, bikes'). Two proactive moments stood out: she gave him a real benchmark instead of a guess — '1700 square foot house typically has 55 to 65 boxes, do you think you're going to be within that range?' — and she corrected a live misconception when he said 'you all had to charge like a minimum of five hours or four hours,' answering 'we have a two and a half hour minimum' and then explaining 'let's say I quote you nine hours but the move took five hours, you only pay for five hours.' That is the kind of specific, honest correction that builds trust.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: this customer told you he was already sold — 'we're going to use you all regardless' — and you let him off the phone unbooked. That is the single most expensive thirty seconds on this call. Right after the recap you should have said: 'Chad, since you already know you're going with us, let me just hold Friday December 11 for you now — there's no deposit, nothing due today, and if anything changes you can move it. Want me to lock it in?' A pre-sold repeat customer with a date is a booking, not a callback. Second priority: he asked for money twice and never got a number. 'I just wanna make sure I have all the money set aside' is a direct request for the rate — you can always give the hourly ($192 for two movers, the Friday tier, plus what's included) even when the total range has to come by email. Third, he handed you the Save Your Ass speech on a platter: he has a truck and a trailer, he's moving close by, and he offered twice to haul boxes himself. That was your opening for 'Every box you and I get out of the way before we show up is time off the clock and money back in your pocket — kids' toys, garden tools, anything loose in drawers, take a carload every time you drive over. Does that make sense?' You gave him the logistics of it ('we can plan on loading the big stuff first') but never the money framing, which is the whole point. BUSINESS RISKS, all three worth Amanda's attention: (1) the customer clearly remembers being charged 'like a minimum of five hours or four hours' on a prior Einstein move — if that's accurate it is a past billing or policy inconsistency against our 2.5-hour minimum and someone should check his old job; (2) she committed to building and sending an estimate with no confirmed destination address, having told him 'the drive time is very close' — trip fee and drive time are unverified assumptions baked into a quote, which is exactly our estimate-accuracy problem; (3) the move date is roughly three months out and the estimate goes out today, so it needs a re-confirmation step before December or the pricing tier and crew availability will both be stale.
phone_presence_notes: Used Chad's name four times naturally and had one nice collaborative beat where she supplied the word he was reaching for ('Yeah, like a TV stand' — 'Yes. Yeah, there you go'), but the acknowledgments were overwhelmingly 'Okay,' 'Got it,' 'Mm-hmm,' with no empathy statement and no response to his one stress cue about setting the money aside.
